chicken-thigh-fried-coated-prepared-skin.title: Chicken thigh, fried, coated, skinless, coating eaten, from raw

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken thigh that has been deep‑fried in a breaded coating. Made from raw product code 846, it retains a high protein level while the coating adds a crunchy texture and extra flavor. This dish is common in main courses, fast‑food menus, and as a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken thighs contain more fat than breast meat, making them juicier when fried.
Deep‑frying at 175‑190 °C creates a golden crust while keeping the interior moist.
The coating can be made from wheat flour, breadcrumbs, spices, and sometimes cornmeal crumbs.
Often served with sauces such as barbecue, honey‑mustard, or garlic aioli.
In some cuisines (e.g., South American) the thighs are marinated in lime and paprika before breading.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides about 20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, essential for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Fatty acids
items.content: The fat retained after frying includes monounsaturated and polyunsaturated acids that, in moderation, are heart‑healthy.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat promotes a lasting feeling of fullness.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Deep‑frying increases calories; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Using oils high in saturated fat can raise cardiovascular risk.

items.title: Food allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to wheat in the breading.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potential carcinogen; avoid over‑cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Breaded chicken thighs are convenient as a hot snack, added to salads, sandwiches, or served with sides such as potatoes, rice, or vegetables. Pair with a variety of dipping sauces to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked product refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight container for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Goat milk is the milk of the domestic goat. It is white, slightly sweet, and has a characteristic mild tang. It is drunk, added to porridge and baked goods, and used to make yogurt, cottage cheese, and cheeses such as chèvre and feta. Goat milk is close to cow milk in composition but differs in the structure of its fat and proteins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The fat globules in goat milk are smaller, so it separates less and mixes more easily.
Goat milk is whiter than cow milk because goats convert beta-carotene into vitamin A.
Goat milk is made into chèvre, feta, and other cheeses.
Goats were among the first domesticated animals.
A goat gives less milk than a cow.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Goat milk provides high-quality protein.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Calcium is needed for bones and teeth.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Contains vitamins A and B2
items.content: These vitamins support vision, skin, and metabolism.

items.title: May be easier to digest
items.content: Some people find goat milk easier on the stomach, but scientific evidence for this is limited.

items.title: Lactose
items.content: Goat milk contains lactose, so it is not suitable for people with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: With an allergy to cow milk proteins, goat milk is usually unsafe too because of cross-reaction.

items.title: Raw milk
items.content: Raw milk may contain Brucella, Campylobacter, and Listeria; it should be boiled or drunk pasteurized.

items.title: For infants
items.content: Ordinary goat milk is not suitable for infants in place of formula; there are special goat milk-based formulas for them.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink goat milk pasteurized or boiled, add it to porridge, cocoa, baked goods, shakes, and smoothies, and make yogurt, cottage cheese, and cheeses from it. Raw milk must be boiled.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store milk in the refrigerator in a closed container and use it by the date on the package; after opening, within a few days. Milk can be frozen. Discard milk that smells sour.

content.title: About
content.content: Pretzel chips are crunchy slices of dough formed into small pieces and baked until golden. They contain no added flavors, offering a neutral, slightly salty taste typical of traditional plain pretzels.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The firm texture is achieved by double‑baking at high temperature.
The classic pretzel knot symbolizes infinity, but chips are usually rectangular or triangular.
Pretzel chips are often used as a base for sauces and dips because of their neutral flavor profile.
In the United States they are a popular bar snack, while in Europe they often accompany cheese platters.
One legend says the pretzel shape represents crossed arms of medieval brewers.

items.title: Low in sugar
items.content: Pretzel chips contain virtually no sugar, making them suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: The dough provides slowly released energy.

items.title: Contains small amounts of iron
items.content: Iron is essential for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions add fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Unlike many other snack foods, they are typically baked with little added oil.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Made from wheat flour, pretzel chips can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Even without flavorings, they are often salted; those monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While less fatty than potato chips, they still provide a notable amount of calories.

items.title: Risk of overeating
items.content: The crunchy texture can lead to rapid consumption of large quantities.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pretzel chips can be enjoyed straight from the bag, paired with dips (cheese, hummus, guacamole) or added to salads for extra crunch. Their sturdy packaging makes them convenient for on‑the‑go snacking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chips in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, store them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness. Avoid moisture, which will make them soft.

content.title: About
content.content: Borscht is a traditional Eastern European soup made with beetroot, meat, cabbage and other vegetables. It has a vivid red color, a rich flavor, and is often served with sour cream and fresh herbs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Borscht originated in Ukraine and is considered a national dish.
Traditional recipes use a meat broth, but vegetarian versions are common.
Beetroot gives the soup its characteristic red hue and is high in beta‑carotene.
Regional variations exist: Russian borscht often includes beans, Polish versions may add mushrooms.
Borscht can be served cold in summer and hot in winter.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Beetroot contains betalains, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Cabbage and carrots provide dietary fiber that promotes healthy bowel function.

items.title: Source of vitamins
items.content: Borscht supplies vitamin C, vitamin B6 and folate, important for immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When prepared with moderate meat, borscht remains a low‑fat dish.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: The high liquid content helps maintain the body’s water balance.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Traditional recipes often use a lot of salt, which may be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beef, pork, or certain vegetables.

items.title: Nitrate content
items.content: Beetroot can contain nitrates; excessive intake may lead to nitrite formation.

items.title: Calorie increase with sour cream
items.content: Adding sour cream raises calories and saturated fat levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve borscht hot, typically topped with a dollop of sour cream, fresh dill or parsley, and a slice of rye bread. Optional additions include boiled eggs or beans for extra protein.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. When frozen, it keeps for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating.
